title: The Nightingale Vanishes
tagline: A jewelled clockwork bird sat in a locked vault all week. On appraisal night it turned out to be a fake. Someone switched it — but when?
setting: The Ravel Gallery, a private gallery of decorative arts, during the week of an insurance appraisal.
briefing: On Thursday at 21:40, insurance appraiser Odile Marchetti examined the Ravel Gallery's prize piece — the Nightingale, a nineteenth-century jewelled clockwork bird insured for 3.5 million — in the gallery's vault and declared it a replica. The real bird is gone. The vault was locked all week and nobody reported a break-in. In the previous ten days the bird had been out for restoration and returned on Monday night; the vault was also opened in the small hours of Wednesday. Gallery owner Lucien Ravel recently raised the insurance cover. Restorer Irene Vance had the bird in her studio. Security consultant Felix Dorn built the vault system. Find out when the switch happened, who made it, and whether anyone should be charged.

forensicBrief: The fake is my best witness. Every replica carries the hand of whoever made it — the enamel, the tool marks, the casting seams. Get me the bird, the case, every log that touched that vault, and I will tell you who could have made it.
Nobody broke in, so the records will tell us more than the lock. I want the vault log, the camera files, and the replica itself, sealed and logged. I'll report what they show and nothing more.
prosecutionOpening: The Nightingale did not fly out of a locked vault. Someone carried it out in plain sight and left a forgery singing in its place.
The Nightingale did not leave a locked vault by itself. The evidence will show who took it, and when.

sentences.theft: For the theft of an object of this value I sentence you to six years' imprisonment, and I make a confiscation order.
